## TL;DR

A bad link in the web UI had two silent failures. Unknown paths redirected to the dashboard, so the user never learned the link was wrong. A `?task=` id the board does not have showed the queue with no message on desktop, and the param stayed in the URL. I replaced the redirect with a plain-English "This page doesn't exist" view with a way back, and gave the desktop Work page a "This task isn't on the board" notice with a Back to Work control. Both are covered by a route-table test and a headless WebKit layout check at 375, 768 and 1280 px. The QA write-up is in `docs/qa/2026-11-deep-links-404-qa.md`. Several rows (archived tasks, wrong tab ids, Settings deep links, reload) were checked by reading the code, not by driving a browser, and the QA doc says so.

## Work and rationale

The brief asked for a QA pass across 404s, deleted or archived task links, wrong tab ids, Settings deep links and reload, with fixes and tests. I started by reading the router, the Work view's `?task=` and `?tab=` handling, the Settings query handling, and the existing `*-qa-browser.test.ts` suites.

The router was the clearest defect. `{ path: "/:pathMatch(.*)*", redirect: "/" }` hides a mistyped URL. I replaced it with a `not-found` named route that loads `NotFoundView.vue`. The view stays inside the app shell so the nav still works, and it shows `route.fullPath` so the user can see what they typed. It offers "Go to Work" and "Dashboard". The auth guard still runs first, so a signed-out visitor still lands on `/login` with a `redirect` query.

The Work page had a quieter gap. On the phone layout, an unknown `?task=` already shows a "Task unavailable" shell with Return to Work. On desktop, `openFromTaskParam` fails the fetch, returns, and renders nothing about it. I added `missingTaskId`, set only when the request token still matches so a stale failure can't overwrite a newer lookup. It clears when the param goes away, when a new lookup starts, and on a successful open. The desktop banner clears the param with the existing `returnToQueue`.

For the two notices I made a small `RouteNotice.vue` component (title, one line of explanation, a slot for actions). Both the not-found view and the Work banner use it. Styles are global `.route-notice*` rules in `style.css`, not scoped. That was a deliberate choice: it lets the headless WebKit check render the real markup with the built stylesheet and no scoped-CSS compilation step.

Archived tasks needed no code change. `repo.archivedTasks` filters the same `repo.tasks` list (`isArchived`), so an archived id opens its drawer like any other task. Unknown tab ids are rejected by `tabFromQuery` and the drawer keeps its default tab. Settings already falls back to General for an unknown `tab` and ignores an unknown `section`. I confirmed these by reading the code and recorded them as such.

Tests: `router-not-found.test.ts` checks that unknown paths resolve to `not-found` with no redirect, and that real routes (including query strings and `/tasks/:id/diff`) still resolve to their names. `deep-links-404-qa-browser.test.ts` mounts the real `NotFoundView` and a notice built on `RouteNotice`, lays them out in headless WebKit at three widths, and asserts the page never widens, the way-back controls are inside the viewport, and the expected copy and links are present. Playwright uses only fixture markup. No server, login or visible browser is involved.

The scoped check (`REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`) passed: format, lint, build, CSS layers, theme and hard-coded colour guards, the rendered contrast audit and the UI smoke test. That run marked the test step as skipped (it reports tests as run on the remote validation runner), so I also ran the UI vitest project directly.

## Approaches tried

I first considered rewriting the Work page's `?task=` flow so an unknown id clears the param and shows a toast. I dropped that. The phone shell already keeps the param so the failed link stays inspectable, and a toast disappears before someone reading a shared link sees it. A persistent notice in the page is clearer and matches the phone behaviour.

I also considered a full end-to-end test that mounts `WorkView` with a fake repo store and a stubbed `/api/tasks/:id` 404. Mounting the page pulls in the board, stores and drawer, and the fixtures would have been large and brittle. I kept the browser check on the notice markup, which is the part a user sees, and documented the drawer path as code-read.

For the router test I first tried mounting the router with a mocked `vue-router`. That breaks `createRouter`, so the route-table test lives in its own file with the real `vue-router`.

## Challenges and blockers

The UI vitest project (`vite.config.ts`) runs the whole suite, not just `src/ui-app/tests`, and the root `vitest` binary without `--config` fails to parse `.vue` imports. I used `bunx vitest run --config src/ui-app/vite.config.ts`.

A full UI-project run had 11 failing tests across 8 files. They are in agent-review, branch-artifact-guard, check-timing-recording, cli-control-api, engineer-resources, models, runtime and shot-capture-single. None of them references the Work page, the router, `RouteNotice` or the new view, and rerunning just those 8 files gave the same result. The errors look environmental: temp-directory `ENOTEMPTY`, a missing opencode binary, Bun re-exec and Node module resolution. I did not run them against main to prove they fail there too, so that is unverified. The UI-only tests, including the existing 375 px browser suites, pass. One earlier 375 px run failed on a timing assertion under load and passed on the next run.

Playwright needed the built stylesheet, so the browser suite reads `dist/ui/assets` after `bun run build:ui`, as the existing QA suites do. It also depends on the WebKit browser that Playwright installed earlier.

## Key learnings

A silent redirect is a UX bug, not a convenience. The catch-all hid every bad link, and the only cue was the page changing. A named not-found route costs one component and a test.

A desktop fallback should match the phone fallback. The phone already showed "Task unavailable" with a way back, and the desktop path showed nothing. Checking both layouts for each deep-link case was the quickest way to see the gap.

Keeping the shared notice's styles global made the layout check cheap and honest: WebKit renders the same markup and CSS the app ships. Scoped styles would have needed a compile step inside the test.

Open items for a human: a live, logged-in click-through of the drawer for deleted, archived and wrong-tab links, and a phone touch-target check on hardware, are both recorded in the QA doc as not run here.
